Radiation colitis, chronic. Chronic radiation colitis is expected at > 6 months postradiation therapy. Sections show ulcerations, mild epithelial atypia, architectural changes and atrophy. The lamina propria contains fibrosis, mild chronic inflammation and fibroblast atypia (enlarged hyperchromatic nuclei). The vasculature within submucosal and deeper layers contains hyalinization of vessel wall and intimal thickening. Vascular ectasia, narrowing and thrombosis can also be present. Collagenous colitis (answer A) typically presents with history of watery diarrhea and a > 10 μM subepithelial collagen table (collagenous band). Infection (bacterial) (answer B) will present with an acute clinical history (example: diarrhea and vomiting) after an inciting event (example: food consumption, travel). Acute colitis and granulomas can sometimes be seen. Viral infections (example: cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus) can occur in immunocompromised patients (example: HIV or transplant) and will contain atypical cells with nuclear changes. Mucosal prolapse (answer C) can present endoscopically as a polyp and contains ingrowth of thick muscle bundles that can mechanically squeeze ensnared epithelium. This is accompanied by variable inflammation, ulceration and reaction epithelial change. Acute radiation colitis (answer D) is expected at < 6 months postradiation therapy. The inflammation is typically eosinophilic (characteristic) with eosinophilic cryptitis, crypt abscesses and lamina propria eosinophilia. Sections demonstrate reduced mitotic activity, apoptosis, reduced goblet cell mucin, goblet cell swelling, degenerative changes and atypia (nuclear enlargement and malorientation).

It is well documented that patients with left sided ulcerative colitis may have discontinuous involvement of the periappendiceal or cecal mucosa, known as a cecal patch. TCLBs (formerly known as Wagner-Meissner corpuscles) are Schwannian mechanoreceptors found primarily in the skin and not normally present in the gastrointestinal tract (GIT). TCLBs in the GIT likely arise as a response to mucosal injury. TCLBs are incidentally discovered during endoscopy where they are most often associated with normal mucosa; however, they can also present as polyps. Histologically, TCLBs are seen as nodules within the lamina propria with lamellated or fibrillary eosinophilic cytoplasm. TCLBs are S100 protein positive, which helps distinguish them from some of their histologic mimics, including amyloid (Congo red+, S100-) and granulomata (CD68+, S100-). No treatment is required as TCLBs are benign.

TCLBs are most often incidental findings associated with an endoscopically normal mucosal appearance; however, in some cases they may appear as polyps (A). stem: Which of the following category of medications contains agents that are implicated in pill fragment associated colitis?

options.explanation: Incorrect because these agents are not implicated in pill fragment associated colitis. Bisphosphonates are used to manage low bone density in patients with inflammatory bowel disease and are not associated with an increased risk of gastrointestinal complications in this population. Fibrates are used to treat dyslipidemia and are associated with drug induced colitis but pill fragments are not typically seen histologically. Selective estrogen receptor modulators (SERMs) are a group of hormonal therapy drugs used to treat ovulatory dysfunction, osteoporosis and breast cancer. SERMs may cause some GI symptoms like nausea but are not associated with colitis.

stem: An HIV positive patient with a history of multiple other sexually transmitted infections presents with a 2 month history of an enlarging, now 5 cm scrotal lesion. A punch biopsy is performed and reveals notable squamous hyperplasia and lymphoplasmacytic inflammation but no evidence of carcinoma or viral cytopathic effect. HPV PCR taken of the lesion is negative. A subsequent surgical excision of the mass lesion is performed and shows the findings in the image above. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.explanation: This option is incorrect. Review the correct-answer explanation and the linked PathologyOutlines topic for why this distractor does not fit.

Hypertrophic herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection. In immunocompromised individuals, especially those with HIV, HSV can present in a hypertrophic form as a slowly enlarging mass-like lesion. Biopsy may show squamous hyperplasia and dense lymphoplasmacytic inflammation but viral cytopathic effect may be absent or focal and only evident in larger or excisional specimens. The lesion is often mistaken clinically and histologically for a tumor. The negative HPV PCR helps rule out other viral etiologies and the ultimate diagnosis is frequently confirmed on surgical excision. Answer A is incorrect because condyloma acuminatum is caused by low risk HPV types (most often 6 and 11) and typically shows papillomatosis, koilocytosis and hyperkeratosis on histology. It does not usually present with a dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate or marked squamous hyperplasia without HPV evidence and HPV PCR would be expected to be positive. Answer C is incorrect because IgG4 related disease typically presents with storiform fibrosis, obliterative phlebitis and an increased number of IgG4 positive plasma cells, none of which were reported in the biopsy. Additionally, IgG4 related disease does not usually involve the scrotal skin with squamous hyperplasia or present as a large solitary epidermal mass. Answer D is incorrect because fungal infections typically show granulomatous inflammation, necrosis and identifiable fungal organisms, often highlighted with special stains. These features were not present in this biopsy and the pattern of inflammation and epithelial hyperplasia is more characteristic of a viral (rather than fungal) etiology.

The immune dysfunction in these patients leads to an exaggerated response to HSV infection, resulting in mass forming lesions that may clinically mimic tumors, particularly in the anogenital region. While a high BMI may influence general immune function, there is no evidence that it contributes to the development of these lesions. Answer C is incorrect because tobacco use is not a known risk factor for hypertrophic HSV infection. It is more commonly associated with malignancies (particularly squamous cell carcinoma) but has no established connection to this viral condition. Answer D is incorrect because sun exposure is associated with ultraviolet (UV) induced skin damage and skin cancers, particularly in sun exposed areas. Hypertrophic HSV typically occurs in mucocutaneous or anogenital sites and has no association with sun exposure. Answer E is incorrect because although the exact pathophysiology is not fully defined, there is a well established association with immunosuppression, particularly in patients with HIV; therefore, known risk factors do exist.

Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) is a sexually transmitted infection caused by invasive serovars (L1 - L3) of Chlamydia trachomatis . It primarily affects men who have sex with men and is characterized by ulcerative proctitis, often with pain, rectal bleeding and tender inguinal lymphadenopathy. Imaging may show rectal wall thickening and lymphadenopathy, mimicking malignancy or inflammatory bowel disease. Histologically, LGV typically shows ulceration, dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates, cryptitis and sometimes granulomas. stem: Which of the following features best distinguishes Buschke-Löwenstein tumor from verrucous squamous carcinoma?

options.explanation: HPV ISH positivity. Buschke-Löwenstein tumor is an HPV related neoplasm whereas verrucous carcinoma is not, so HPV ISH staining (positive) would be expected with Buschke-Löwenstein tumor but not with verrucous carcinoma. Buschke-Löwenstein tumor is most often due to a low risk HPV type, such as HPV 6 or 11. Invasive or displacing type growth can be seen in either lesion.

options.text: Reactive lymphadenopathy related to tumor associated infection
options.explanation: Reactive lymphadenopathy related to tumor associated infection. Buschke-Löwenstein tumor is frequently associated with fistulae and perirectal or peritumoral abscess formation, which can lead to regional lymphadenopathy. Metastasis is very uncommon. While immunocompromise may predispose to development of Buschke-Löwenstein tumor, the cause is infrequently due to a lymphoproliferative disorder that would enlarge the lymph nodes. Netherton syndrome is not primarily associated with adenopathy.
